blocks.value: A `switch` statement allows a single variable to be tested for equality against a list of values and, depending on its value, executes a certain block of statements. Each value is a **case**, and the variable being switched on is checked against each one.

items: The variable used in a `switch` can only be of type `int`, `byte`, `short`, `char`, or `String`. *(Also `enum` and the wrapper classes such as `Integer`. Enums are covered in Lesson 18.)*
There can be any number of `case` statements. Each `case` is followed by the value to compare against and a colon.
The value in a `case` must be the **same data type** as the switch variable, and must be a constant.
When the switch variable equals a case, the statements following that case execute **until a `break` is reached**.
When `break` is reached, the switch terminates and control jumps to the next line following the switch. *(A `break` can only terminate an enclosing `switch` or a repetition structure.)*
**Not every case needs a `break`.** If none appears, control **falls through** to subsequent cases until a `break` is reached.
A switch may or may not have a `default`, which must appear at the end. It performs a task when none of the cases match. No `break` is needed in `default`.

Cases 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, and 12 have no statements between them, so control falls straight through to `days = 31`. This is intentional. An **accidental** fall-through: forgetting a `break`, is a different story, and one of the most common switch bugs.

Use `switch` when testing **one variable** against **several fixed values**. Use an `else-if` chain for **ranges** or **conditions involving more than one variable**. The grade-from-score example cannot be a switch, because `score >= 90` is a range, not a single value.
